Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . items.summary: View CSAF Summary Mendix Studio Pro contains multiple vulnerabilities in the MCP Server, that could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the server remotely or trick a user's browser into sending unauthorized requests, potentially leading to unauthorized data access, tool execution, or system compromise. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. The following versions of Siemens Mendix Studio Pro are affected: Mendix Studio Pro 11 vers:intdot/>=11.15.0|<11.16.0 (CVE-2026-112136, CVE-2026-112137) Mendix Studio Pro 11.12 vers:intdot/>=11.12.6|<11.12.7 (CVE-2026-112136, CVE-2026-112137) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Siemens Mendix Studio Pro 11 2 Vulnerabilities Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-112136 The affected products MCP Server does not properly restrict its HTTP listener to the loopback interface, leaving it potentially exposed to remote systems. This could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the MCP Server remotely. Read More 2 Affected Products Mendix Studio Pro 11 >= V11.15.0 < V11.16.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Maintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules. Vendor fix Update to V11.16.0 or later version Mendix Studio Pro 11.12 >= V11.12.6 < V11.12.7 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Maintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules. Vendor fix Update to V11.12.7 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-1327 Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 8.8 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H View CVE Details CVE-2026-112137 The affected products MCP Server does not properly validate Content-Type and Origin headers on incoming HTTP requests, leaving it vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). This could allow a malicious web page to trick a user's browser into sending unauthorized requests and executing unintended actions on the local MCP Server. Read More 4 Affected Products Mendix Studio Pro 11 >= V11.15.0 < V11.16.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Utilize modern Chromium- or WebKit-based browsers with Private Network Access protections enabled, or use browser extensions (such as uBlock Origin or NoScript) to block external websites from issuing fetch requests to localhost (127.0.0.1). Vendor fix Update to V11.16.0 or later version Mendix Studio Pro 11.12 >= V11.12.6 < V11.12.7 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Utilize modern Chromium- or WebKit-based browsers with Private Network Access protections enabled, or use browser extensions (such as uBlock Origin or NoScript) to block external websites from issuing fetch requests to localhost (127.0.0.1). items.summary: Purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938 . This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. Resources CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates: Vendor Guidance Oracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Update – November 2026 Disclaimer The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. CISA does not endorse any commercial entity, product, company, or service, including any entities, products, or services linked within this document. Any reference to specific commercial entities, products, processes, or services by service mark, trademark, manufacturer, or otherwise, does not constitute or imply endorsement, recommendation, or favoring by CISA. Acknowledgements The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cyber Centre) contributed to this Alert.

General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. items.summary:
### Impact
The AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper is an open-source JDBC driver wrapper that extends a JDBC driver to enable Amazon Aurora and AWS Cloud features such as failover handling and caching. We identified CVE-2026-14265, an issue in the RemoteQueryCachePlugin of the AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper. When this plugin is enabled, query results read from the shared Redis/Valkey cache are deserialized without class filtering. An actor with write access to the shared cache infrastructure could insert a crafted serialized Java object that, when read by an application, results in execution of arbitrary code on the application server.

### Workarounds
The RemoteQueryCachePlugin is not enabled by default. Customers who cannot immediately upgrade can mitigate this issue by disabling the RemoteQueryCachePlugin, and by restricting write access to the Redis/Valkey cache infrastructure to trusted principals.

items.summary: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Philips Hue Bridge HomeKit Accessory Protocol chacha20_decrypt Integer Underflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Philips Hue Bridge. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the HomeKit Accessory Protocol service, which listens on TCP port 8080 by default. When parsing pairing requests, the process does not properly validate user-supplied data, which can result in an integer underflow before writing to memory. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-28332.

items.summary:
### Impact

Two effects, sharing the root cause of Advisory 1 — header names chosen by the sender were
resolved through Python attribute lookup and rewritten before lookup.

**Uncaught exceptions.** A crafted message raises an exception that is *outside* the
`MailParser*` hierarchy, so a caller catching only mail-parser exceptions does not catch it
and the worker dies.

*Header named after a method* (CWE-248, reported by @iam-niranjan). Python resolves real
class attributes before `__getattr__`, so a header named after a method put a bound method
object into the parsed mail dict. A 12-byte email is sufficient. Nine colliding names were
confirmed: `Parse`, `Message`, `Write_Attachments`, `From_File`, `From_File_Obj`,
`From_File_Msg`, `From_String`, `From_Bytes`, `Get_Server_Ipaddress`. Also reproducible from
the CLI (`mail-parser -f evil.eml -j`).

```python
import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_string("Parse: x\r\n\r\n").mail_json
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type method is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> {"parse": "x", "has_defects": false}
```

*Header carrying 8-bit bytes* (CWE-248). For a header containing raw 8-bit bytes, Python's
`compat32` policy returns an `email.header.Header` rather than a `str`, which the `_raw`
accessor passed straight to `json.dumps`. This fires on entirely benign non-ASCII mail via
`parse_from_bytes()`, the normal entry point for mail off the wire.

```python
import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_bytes(b"Subject: caf\xe9\r\n\r\nbody\r\n").subject_raw
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type Header is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> '["caf�"]'
```

**Silent loss of message content** (CWE-436). A sender can make a header's value vanish from
every output surface, or be replaced by a different header's value, with `has_defects`
remaining `false`. This is an evasion primitive: the tool's output diverges from the bytes
actually in the message, and a pipeline scanning parsed output for indicators sees nothing
and no failure signal.

Header names were normalised before lookup — underscores folded to dashes, and `_json` /
`_raw` suffixes interpreted — so a header genuinely named `Subject_json` was reported with
the value of `Subject` and its own value discarded, and any header whose name contains an
underscore resolved to nothing.

```python
import mailparser

raw = ("From: Real Sender <real@good.example>\r\n"
       "Subject: innocuous\r\n"
       "Subject_json: MALWARE-C2 http://evil.example/payload.exe\r\n"
       "X_Spam_Flag: YES\r\n\r\nbody\r\n")
mail = mailparser.parse_from_string(raw)
print(mail.mail["subject_json"])       # 4.6.1 -> '"innocuous"'   4.6.2 -> the real value
print(mail.headers["X_Spam_Flag"])     # 4.6.1 -> ''              4.6.2 -> 'YES'
print("MALWARE-C2" in mail.mail_json)  # 4.6.1 -> False           4.6.2 -> True
print(mail.has_defects)                # both  -> False
```

A related case: `email.message.Message.__len__` returns the header count, so a message with
**no headers** is falsy. `parse()` returned before initialising state, and the unset
attributes were then absorbed by `__getattr__` and answered as absent headers. Every
property returned `''` — including `mail` and `attachments`, which are documented to return
a `dict` and a `list` — with no error and no defect flag.

```python
import mailparser
mail = mailparser.parse_from_string("Click http://evil.example/pay.exe now\r\n")
print(repr(mail.body))         # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> the text
print(repr(mail.attachments))  # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> []
print(mail.has_defects)        # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> True
```

Fixed in **4.6.2**. Upgrade with `pip install --upgrade mail-parser`.

Header names taken from a message are now looked up literally — no attribute access, no
case or separator folding, no suffix interpretation — so no header name can collide with a
method or property, and no value can be substituted or dropped. 8-bit values are coerced to
`str` before serialisation. Parser state is initialis

items.summary: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.
items.title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study

items.summary: The key agreements that protect a Wi-Fi connection rely on Diffie-Hellman, which a sufficiently capable quantum computer would break; an adversary can therefore record an association today and decrypt its traffic years later. Key establishment is thus the part of IEEE 802.11 that has to be migrated first. This work targets the two protocols that perform that agreement inside the frames used to set up the link: Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE), which encrypts otherwise open networks, and Fast Initial Link Setup (FILS), designed for fast connection in dense and mobile deployments. We propose replacing their Diffie-Hellman exchange with a hybrid one that runs the classical elliptic-curve agreement alongside ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and derives the master key from both secrets, so the connection stays protected as long as either component remains unbroken. The exchange reuses the frames each protocol already sends and adds no extra round trip; an access point can advertise the hybrid mode alongside classical OWE, and a station configured to require it refuses to associate without a completed post-quantum exchange. Binding the advertised capabilities to the derived key is specified as a design extension and is not part of the prototype. We validate the design with a working implementation on hostapd and wpa_supplicant: both endpoints derive the same key in every measured connection, with the two smaller parameter sets each enlarged association frame fits in a single frame even under a conservative 1500-byte fragmentation threshold, and the added connection time and computation stay below half a millisecond. The measurements are obtained on OWE; the design carries over to FILS, whose frame budget is left for specific measurement. Of the three ML-KEM parameter sets, the intermediate one offers the best balance between security level and size.
items.title: Post-Quantum Migration of Wi-Fi Key Establishment: A Hybrid ML-KEM Design for OWE and FILS, Validated on OWE with hostapd

items.summary: Significant privacy and copyright concerns are raised by the use of publicly available audio recordings to train audio large language models (LLMs), yet effective auditing methods remain limited. Existing membership inference attacks typically assume knowledge of complete training examples, including their associated textual supervision. In practice, however, audio recordings may be paired with privately generated transcripts, captions, or question-answer pairs that are unavailable to owners of the recordings. This motivates audio-file-level membership inference, which determines whether a recording was used for training without assuming knowledge of its training tasks and annotations. This paper provides the first systematic investigation of this challenge and introduces AudioTraceBench, a controlled benchmark comprising 1,285 audio recordings with explicit fine-tuning membership labels. Evaluations across three audio LLMs show that existing text- and video-based membership inference methods adapted to audio perform close to random guessing. To address this challenge, AudioTrace is proposed, where audio-conditioned proxy questions are generated using the target model, and membership evidence is extracted from its responses and aggregated at the recording level. Consistent improvements over existing baselines are observed, with AUROC reaching 0.60 and increasing further under increased fine-tuning exposure or adaptation capacity. Further experiments were conducted to examine the factors influencing membership signals for audio-file-level detection. These findings establish audio-file-level membership inference as a distinct and practically important auditing challenge, with AudioTrace providing an effective initial approach to this challenge.
items.title: AudioTrace: File-Level Membership Detection for Audio Large Language Models

items.summary: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition. On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. items.summary:
This is a Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) vulnerability stemming from improper symlink handling (CWE-59: Link Following) and improper ownership management (CWE-282) inside the qbee-agent file manager logic.

### Impact

Any managed device running qbee-agent up to the affected versions. The impact manifests in three distinct vectors:

1. **Primary Vector (Full Privilege Escalation to Root - Default Configuration)**: If an unprivileged user's account is managed by the SSH Keys bundle, they can replace or remove their own `~/.ssh` directory and create a symlink pointing to `/root/.ssh`. On the next configuration apply, qbee-agent follows the symlink and writes the user's server-provisioned public key directly into `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Since the symlink resides inside the user's own home directory, kernel protections like `fs.protected_symlinks` do not block this execution. The attacker can then instantly log in as root via SSH.

2. **Secondary Vector (Arbitrary File Overwrite / DoS via RAUC Staging)**: On devices utilizing RAUC download mode, the agent uses a predictable, world-writable staging path (`/tmp/.bundle.raucb.part`). If `fs.protected_symlinks` is disabled `(0)`, an unprivileged user can symlink this path to a vital system file (e.g., `/etc/shadow` or `/etc/pam.d/*`), causing the agent to truncate or overwrite it with server-supplied update data during a RAUC update deployment.

3. **Tertiary Vector (Arbitrary File Re-ownership via File Distribution)**: If an operator configures a file-distribution/template destination under a directory owned by an unprivileged user, the attacker can create a symlink at the partial download path targeting a sensitive system file. The agent will then inadvertently execute `file.Chown()` on the targeted file, handing ownership over to the unprivileged attacker.

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed by hardening file creation and directory traversal inside `app/configuration/file_manager.go`. Specifically, the agent now enforces `syscall.O_NOFOLLOW` and proper existence validation flags during privileged operations to prevent link resolution outside intended directories.

Users should upgrade to version 2026.27 (or newer) to fully mitigate these vectors.

### Workarounds

If upgrading immediately is not feasible, administrators can apply the following mitigations:

1. Disable the SSH Keys Bundle: Temporarily turn off SSH key management within the Qbee platform for non-trusted local accounts to eliminate the primary privilege escalation vector.

2. Restrict Local Home Directory Alterations: Enforce strict file permissions or monitoring on managed user home directories to block unprivileged users from deleting or replacing ~/.ssh with a symbolic link.

3. Enable Kernel Symlink Protection: Ensure that system-level symlink protections are active to mitigate the secondary `/tmp` vector by verifying that the following sysctl parameter is set to 1 (though note this does not fix the primary home directory vector):

```bash
sysctl -w fs.protected_symlinks=1
```

items.summary:
### Patches

Fixed in **4.6.2**. Upgrade with `pip install --upgrade mail-parser`.

Candidate addresses are now selected by position, not by appearance — a bracketed address
the sender wrote is byte-identical to one the MTA wrote, so no amount of pattern matching
can tell them apart:

- the first token of the `from` clause is the HELO name, whatever its shape, and is never a
  candidate;
- an explicit HELO marker inside a comment group is sender text and is excluded;
- a candidate must sit inside a `(` / `[` group;
- IPv4 and IPv6 matches are merged positionally, never family-first;
- the walk stops at the first trusted hop naming no address, rather than continuing into
  sender-written headers.

The IPv6 pattern was corrected to skip the `IPv6:` tag and to prefer the longest valid form.

**Behaviour change.** `get_server_ipaddress()` now returns `None` rather than an unreliable
value in two cases that previously returned an address: a `from` clause consisting of a bare
address with no HELO marker (indistinguishable from `EHLO <that address>`), and a trusted hop
naming no address at all. Callers must handle `None`.

### Workarounds

None within mail-parser. Callers who cannot upgrade should not treat the return value of
`get_server_ipaddress()` as trustworthy, and should derive sender attribution from an
authenticated signal instead — the MTA's own logs, or SPF/DKIM/DMARC results computed
outside this library.

items.summary:
termux-sync restore trusts fields inside an untrusted backup manifest and uses them as the extraction destination without validation.

During restore, each archive entry is handled as:

  src_dir = Path(info.get("source", ...)).parent
  extract_archive(archive, src_dir, ...)

extract_archive opens the archive and runs tarfile.extract for every member with no path jail and no filter:

  with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:*") as tf:
      for member in tf.getmembers():
          tf.extract(member, dest_path, set_attrs=True)

There is no check that manifest "source" stays under an expected restore root, that tar members stay inside dest_path, or that backup_name used in temporary paths cannot contain ".." or separators.

Impact:
A victim who restores a malicious backup (local, shared, or from a compromised GitHub/Google Drive storage backend) can have arbitrary files written anywhere the Termux user can write. Overwriting shell startup files or executable scripts leads to local code execution on later use.

Reproduction (benign markers only):

1. Build a backup directory with home.tar.gz (members: proof filename + optional config names) and manifest.json.
2. Set files.home.source to any path whose parent is the desired write directory (e.g. $HOME/dummy_for_parent so parent is $HOME).
3. Run the same extract path the tool uses: src_dir = Path(source).parent; tarfile.extract each member into src_dir.
4. Observe attacker-controlled files created under $HOME and under other chosen roots (config / shell-rc style overwrite).

Expected: restore only writes under fixed, validated roots; reject unsafe source values and members that resolve outside dest.
Actual: write destination is fully controlled by manifest.source; proof files and overwrites appear outside any intended jail.

Fix direction:
- Do not trust manifest "source" for extract roots; use fixed app-defined destinations
- Sanitize backup_name (basename; reject ".." and separators)
- Extract with tarfile filter="data" (or equivalent boundary checks) and refuse escape
- Treat backups as untrusted input

Actual result (local marker-only reproduction):

PROOF path: /data/data/com.termux/files/home/PWNED_BY_TERMUX_SYNC_RESTORE.txt
PROOF exists? True
PROOF content:
PWNED
This file was written by a malicious termux-sync backup restore path.
Root cause: manifest files.*.source controls extract destination.

*** VULN CONFIRMED: arbitrary write to $HOME ***

important.conf => secret=ATTACKER_CONTROLLED
*** VULN CONFIRMED: overwrite under attacker-chosen root ***

.bashrc_sim shows injected:
export ATTACKER=1
*** VULN CONFIRMED: startup-file style overwrite ***

Extract roots used:
  home  -> parent($HOME/dummy_for_parent) = $HOME
  config -> parent(.../victim_sim/nested_dummy) = .../victim_sim

Reported and credited to Niranj R Mahaswar ( GitHub: @NiranjMahaswar )

items.summary:
### Impact

`code-review-mcp-server` exposes MCP tools (`getLocalGitDiff`, `codeReview`, `createPR`, `getPRTemplate`) that accept `folderPath` and `baseBranch` string parameters. These caller-controlled values were interpolated directly into shell command strings executed via `child_process.execSync()`, which runs commands through `/bin/sh`.

A crafted value such as `baseBranch = "main; <arbitrary command> #"` (or a `$(...)` command substitution, or a `folderPath` that breaks out of the surrounding quotes) results in **arbitrary command execution** on the host running the MCP server.

### Patches

Fixed in **1.5.3**. Every `execSync()` call was replaced with `execFileSync()` using argument arrays, so inputs are passed directly to `git` / `gh` without going through a shell, eliminating the injection at its root.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to `code-review-mcp-server@1.5.3` or later.

### Summary

LightSaml 5.0.0 (latest release; also confirmed on 4.6.1) validates an inbound `samlp:Response` by collecting its direct-child `saml:Assertion` elements and validating each one's `ds:Signature` via robrichards/xmlseclibs. The two layers disagree on which element a signature actually covers: LightSaml reads claims from the assertion node it collected, while xmlseclibs resolves the signed `Reference URI="#id"` with a document-wide `//*[@Id]` XPath that returns the first ID-bearing element anywhere in the document.

An attacker who has captured one genuine signed assertion can exploit this to surface attacker-authored, unsigned claims.

### Details

`Response::deserialize` collects assertions with `manyElementsFromXml`, whose relative XPath `saml:Assertion` matches only direct children of the `Response`. Each collected assertion is validated independently by `AssertionSignatureValidatorAction` against the out-of-band trusted IdP credential (resolved by Issuer entityId, never from the document):

https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Model/Protocol/Response.php#L122
https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Model/AbstractSamlModel.php#L93
https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Action/Assertion/Inbound/AssertionSignatureValidatorAction.php#L28

The check delegates to xmlseclibs `XMLSecurityDSig::validateReference()`, which first removes the signature node being validated from the shared document (enveloped-signature removal):

```php
if (! $docElem->isSameNode($this->sigNode)) {
    if ($this->sigNode->parentNode != null) {
        $this->sigNode->parentNode->removeChild($this->sigNode);   // strips sig from shared DOM
    }
}
```

https://github.com/robrichards/xmlseclibs/blob/3.1.5/src/XMLSecurityDSig.php#L596

`processRefNode()` then resolves `URI="#id"` document-wide and takes `item(0)`, the first ID-bearing element in the whole document, any name or namespace, not the one inside the signature's own subtree:

```php
$query = '//*['.$iDlist.']';
$dataObject = $xPath->query($query)->item(0);
```

https://github.com/robrichards/xmlseclibs/blob/3.1.5/src/XMLSecurityDSig.php#L525

https://github.com/litesaml/lightsaml/blob/5.0.0/src/Model/Assertion/Assertion.php#L288

items.summary: virtualenv is a tool for creating isolated virtual python environments. Prior to 21.14.9, download_wheel() writes package-index downloads directly into the reusable wheel/house cache before selecting a verification target from pip's textual Saved output. With default-index digest comparison enabled, a controlled package index can inject a misleading Saved line through a discarded link's data-requires-python attribute; this forged-line variant also requires knowledge of an absolute path to the genuine bundled wheel. The wrong path can then be hashed, while a digest mismatch leaves the rejected archive in the cache for later selection without verification. A separate rejected-cache-file variant requires control over downloaded data or archive selection but not the forged-line prerequisites. Explicit custom-index exceptions are outside the promised PyPI comparison, and the issue does not independently bypass TLS or establish control of default PyPI. items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfrm: iptfs: propagate SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG in iptfs_skb_add_frags()

When iptfs_skb_add_frags() copies frag references from the source
frag walk into a new SKB, it increments the page reference count via
__skb_frag_ref() but does not propagate SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG to the
destination SKB's skb_shinfo->flags.

If the source SKB carries shared frags (e.g. from a page-pool backed
receive path), the new inner SKB will appear to ESP as having privately
owned frags.  A subsequent esp_input() call for a nested transport-mode
SA then takes the no-COW fast path and decrypts in place, writing over
pages that are still referenced by the outer IPTFS SKB.  This causes
kernel-visible memory corruption and can trigger a panic.

All other frag-transfer helpers in the kernel (skb_try_coalesce,
skb_gro_receive, __pskb_copy_fclone, skb_shift, skb_segment) correctly
propagate SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG; align iptfs_skb_add_frags() with this
convention by setting the flag inside the loop immediately after
__skb_frag_ref() and nr_frags++, so every exit path that attaches a frag
unconditionally propagates SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG.

items.summary: A mix-network (mixnet) is a routing network that breaks source-to-destination message trackability by indistinguishably mixing the routes of concurrently transmitted messages, thus providing anonymity to senders, receivers and sender-receiver pairs. Given their potential use in high-stakes scenarios like protecting whistleblowers, one would like to prove formally that sender anonymity holds in a mixnet, even against strong adversaries that can compromise subsets of mixnet servers. However, existing work on anonymity in mixnets is either limited to linear mixnets (which do not scale horizontally), relies on special provisions such as additional noise or chaff messages, or is empirical -- typically based on entropy, which does not provide strong guarantees if the adversary has auxiliary information. In this paper, we present a new analysis of parallel mixnets which scale horizontally, showing that these networks can provide strong indistinguishability for messages even without additional noise messages. Our analysis works by bounding the statistical variance of the adversary's posterior likelihood of where a message of interest is at a given point in time. Using concentration bounds on this distribution, we show that parallel mixnets satisfy $(\varepsilon, δ)$-differential indistinguishability for messages routed through the mixnet (similar to $(\varepsilon, δ)$-differential privacy) with very small failure probabilities $δ$ and small privacy parameters $\varepsilon$ under reasonable operating conditions. Our model also enables an examination of the quantitative trade-off between anonymity, latency and per-router bandwidth in parallel mixnets.
items.title: Provable Mixing Properties of Parallel Mixnets Revisited

items.summary: A pixel-sparse adversary may change a few pixels of an image to any value. Robustness to such attacks is currently measured with an ensemble, sparse-AutoAttack (sAA), because its members fail in different places: sparse projected gradient descent (sPGD) trusts a first-order model that a full pixel change breaks, and sparse random search (Sparse-RS) ignores the gradient even where it is informative. We show that both attacks are local searches, each a proposal distribution plus an acceptance rule, and ask what such a search can learn from the gradient. A Taylor bound says what to measure, and measurements at the states the search visits give five rules. The sign of the gradient is its most reliable use at a single pixel and sets a new pixel's value. Its ranking of candidate pixels should be followed loosely, and its ranking of the pixels to remove, which is often more reliable, can be followed more closely. A pixel should not be proposed twice before a move is accepted, and acceptance should be decided by the loss alone. These rules define Gradient-guided Random Search (GRS), which runs once and costs one forward and one backward pass per step. On 13 CIFAR-10 configurations and 5 ImageNet models, GRS matches or beats the best single member of sAA and is within one point of sAA itself or stronger on 17 of 18 settings, and it is significantly stronger than sAA on 8. It uses 3 instead of up to 7 forward-pass units, and on CIFAR-10 it runs 3.7 to 5.0 times faster than the members of sAA run in full.
items.title: Propose with the Gradient, Accept with the Loss: One Hedged Attack for Pixel-Sparse Robustness

items.summary: Cross-border cyber attacks on European SMEs and critical-infrastructure operators expose a structural cyber-resilience gap: cybersecurity (threat sharing, detection, response), compliance (framework assessment, certification) and digital forensics (cross-jurisdictional evidence) are jointly regulated by NIS2, the CRA, GDPR and the LED, yet their tooling evolved in silos and rarely interoperates across Member States. The EU-funded CYBER-BRIDGE project integrates the three domains under one architecture and a hash-chained evidence layer: AI-driven CTI sharing with ENISA-aligned notification, multi-framework assessments with retrieval-augmented advisory, and RFC 3161-anchored custody with lawful GDPR/LED exchange, all aligned with MITRE ATT&CK. A sanitised replica of the back-end image hosts a Cyber-Range for upskilling. The contribution is not the individual tools but the reconciliation mechanism that lets one incident produce, from a single evidence record, a cross-border CTI advisory, the regulatory notifications its deadlines demand and a re-verifiable forensic pack; we set out why binding three differently regulated evidence regimes onto one record is non-trivial and how the shared evidence layer resolves the resulting tensions. This paper introduces the project's scope, requirements, pilots, architecture and toolkits; quantitative KPIs follow in later deliverables.
items.title: The CYBER-BRIDGE project: An AI-Powered Platform for Cross-Border Cybersecurity, Compliance and Forensics in the EU

items.summary: AI assistants are becoming part of how knowledge workers think and perform, accumulating the prompts, exemplars, memory and interaction histories that encode a worker's professional judgment. This infrastructure typically runs under employer or platform control. We name the resulting process expertise capture, the absorption of worker-applied knowledge and judgment into AI resources under organizational control. We develop a framework of contribution forms, technical residences and transformation families, and show that how far a contribution can be attributed, separated and revoked depends on where it resides and how it has been transformed, properties fixed by system design long before any dispute arises. When a worker departs, the organization retains a capability shaped by their judgment while the worker loses access to it, and the asymmetry compounds as contributions move from inspectable artifacts into derivatives, learned components and successor systems. We outline three measures, write-time provenance, extraction of separable contributions and an executable exit procedure, that make an agreed allocation technically performable, and make explicit what cannot be separated at all.
items.title: Expertise capture in workplace AI

items.summary: Emerging quantum computers threaten to break the classical key exchange algorithms. To safeguard against these threats, migration to new quantum-safe algorithms is underway and expected to be expedited. Though resistant to attacks, the quantum safe algorithms may impact the real-world performance due to their large key lengths. In this work, we analyze the end-to-end performance of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol with the post-quantum (PQ) and hybrid cryptographic algorithms standardized by NIST. We develop a test setup to evaluate the performance of TLS connections between a client and a server under various network conditions. We focus on the impact of the new algorithms on the speed (throughput, connection time) and sustainability (energy, CPU cycles) of TLS 1.3. Our analysis demonstrates that the standardized post-quantum algorithms do not introduce any measurable performance degradations in TLS 1.3, despite their larger key lengths. However, hybrid algorithms introduce noticeable performance degradation, which becomes increasingly pronounced under adverse network conditions. Our analysis suggests that migration to hybrid algorithms should be ``network condition aware'' as poor network conditions can severely degrade performance in TLS 1.3. We provide anonymised link to the code and a web interface to analyse performance of various combination of algorithms.
items.title: PQC Migration: End-to-End Performance Profiling of Post Quantum Cryptographic Algorithms in mTLS

items.summary: The inheritance of crypto-assets faces a structural obstacle: ownership is the knowledge of a key, so the key either disappears with its owner or has to be shared beforehand. The Tales From the Crypt Protocol (TFCP) addressed one part of the problem, the distributed and privacy-preserving acknowledgment of a death by a blockchain. We revisit it with a new primitive. A \emph{baryonic key} is a physical object from which bits are obtained only through a measurement, are never stored digitally, and which exists in exactly $n$ copies, where $n$ is neither zero nor unbounded. We define the primitive, outline a candidate instantiation based on a replicated micro-fractured relief, and state its limits: digitising a copy is slow and tamper-evident, not impossible. We also outline other uses of the primitive, from post-quantum pre-shared keys to common coins for Byzantine agreement. We then give a threat model for TFCP, review the attack models of the literature that apply to it, and show where it resists and where it does not. We propose TFCP-B, in which decrypting the will requires both a secret shared among registrars and the response of a baryonic key, and in which heirs claim their share through hash commitments, without any prior key or wallet. We detail each change from TFCP to TFCP-B, with its rationale and its price. TFCP-B removes the anonymity loss caused by colluding registrars and blocks several false-alarm attacks. It does not remove the shallow-account attack, remains exposed to transaction censorship during the deliberation period, and introduces new assumptions on custodians and reading devices. The security arguments are informal and the physical figures are design estimates.
items.title: Baryonic Keys and the Inheritance of Crypto-Assets: Revisiting the Tales From the Crypt Protocol

items.summary: An enterprise breach causes most of its damage after the perimeter is crossed. Once an attacker gains a foothold, they can move laterally to other hosts, take over the trusted services of the network, and encrypt the backups needed for recovery. Defenders, on the other hand, need to study this post-compromise stage, but they cannot rehearse it on a production enterprise network. Building such an enterprise network manually is time-consuming, and resetting it to its clean state between runs is still harder. As a result, security experiments are difficult to perform, compare and reproduce. We develop Enterprise Network Testbed for Reproducible Attack and Defense Practices (ENTRAP), an Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) cyber range that defines a fully segmented enterprise as version-controlled automation. ENTRAP uses Ansible, KVM/Libvirt, and Cloud-init to provision the environment and reset it to a clean state whenever necessary. The enterprise network includes several entities such as a gateway, an internal Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), DNS, DHCP, a backup server, a web server, and clients. On this network, a user can learn to assemble the entities, launch attacks, and write rules or defensive measures that harden its security. We launch three attacks: a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS)-backed ransomware campaign, a Layer-2 DHCP starvation and rogue DHCP attack, and perimeter web exploitation. Each attack runs from a clean state, and ENTRAP acts as a reproducible generator of labeled attack datasets. Using the collected dataset, we train a Random Forest classifier for ransomware detection and present its evaluation results. We publicly release the codebase, collected logs, and datasets to facilitate further research.
items.title: Experience: ENTRAP - An IaC Enterprise Cyber Range for Reproducible Security Assessment and Dataset Generation

items.summary: Execution traces help diagnose AI-agent failures, but sharing them can expose customer identities. For example, detecting that an agent handled the wrong customer's records requires knowing whether the records belong to the requested customer, but not necessarily knowing who that customer is. Our executable benchmark measures what a trace export reveals and whether a proposed repair restores the correct output in synthetic multi-tenant workflows. Conventional redaction can remove evidence needed for repair while leaving encoded identifiers recoverable. Two exports preserve ownership comparisons by reporting the match as a comparison fact or by using pseudonyms consistent within each execution. Both preserve the original diagnostic program's repairs. The tested identifier matchers identify no requested customer from either export. An independently written program produces correct outputs on 39 of 42 faulty cases with comparison facts and on all 42 with execution-scoped pseudonyms. Row counts still expose identities. With prior knowledge of customers' row counts, an attacker uniquely identifies the requested customer in 97 of 240 executions under each of the 15 export policies. Removing selected counters from the comparison-fact export stops this attack and preserves the original program's repairs. The benchmark lets engineers test what their diagnostic program can repair and what an attacker can still infer from the same export.
items.title: Where the Evidence Lives: Measuring Privacy and Diagnosability of Exported AI-Agent Traces

items.summary: Oracle attacks show the importance of a correct implementation of cryptographic standards when translated into code. A notable example is the Bleichenbacher attack on RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding and all the improvements that have been suggested over the decades. This paper shows how an attacker knowing a few least significant bytes of an RSA message can take advantage of a server with an oracle side-channel to decrypt the full message bit by bit. We will consider two oracles that can be tested with chosen ciphertexts: one revealing whether the decrypted message starts with the 00 02 bytes and a second one revealing if the decrypted message is fully PKCS compliant. For an attacker knowing the three least significant bytes of the message, the first oracle provides an attack where one oracle call gives the next least significant bit of the message and the second an attack which requires, with high probability, a small constant number of oracle calls to the oracle, with a constant which depends on the length of the message and the desired probability of success. The attack divides the message bits into two sections, one with the known part and one with the unknown part, and then chooses transformations that will keep the unknown part, except for the last unknown bit, orders of magnitude below the integer coming from the known part. The resulting string either gives a valid padding or not depending on the value of the unknown bit. The attacker can minimize the number of oracle calls at the cost of some local computation. Finally, the same method is adapted to show how it can also be used to extract the few least significant bytes of the message with an increased cost where the main complexity is finding a second valid message with a correct padding starting from the original captured ciphertext.
items.title: A Bleichenbacher bit-by-bit oracle attack from partial message knowledge

items.summary: The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. Two representative use cases--pilot fatigue and warfighters operating in harsh environments--guide requirements, validation, and interface design (including HUD and haptic feedback). As an initial step toward embedded models, we benchmark stress classification on a public wearable dataset: tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art performance for accuracy and F1 (e.g., XGBoost: $\mathrm{Accuracy}=0.901\!\pm\!0.023$, $\mathrm{F1}=0.920\!\pm\!0.019$), while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC ($0.963\!\pm\!0.025$), informing feature-engineering and compression choices for edge deployment. Building on these results, CAPSARII employs HW/SW co-design, model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), and precision tuning to meet stringent energy and memory budgets; it further investigates Processing-in-Memory accelerators for future efficiency gains. A structured gap analysis highlights the remaining challenges: establishing validation standards for physiological signal quality and textile durability; achieving low-latency, scalable BAN/SAN communications under mobility and interference; and deploying hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography with robust device identity and side-channel resilience on constrained endpoints. By consolidating these elements into a coherent, secure IoBT stack, CAPSARII delineates a practical roadmap from laboratory baselines to mission-ready soldier monitoring in both training and operational scenarios.

items.summary: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
items.title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems

items.summary: Open-weight model hubs now ship not only chat checkpoints but a long tail of derivatives---fine-tunes, safety guards, vision--language models (VLMs), audio wrappers, and generative heads---yet residual-stream safety audits still often intervene at a single site, usually the text decoder $T$. We ask a localization question under one shared mean / rank-1 difference-in-means (DiM) extract$=$intervene protocol, with matched-norm random and empty-rate controls: does causal chat attack lift concentrate at $T$, or do perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E$/$P$/$F$) supply a comparable bypass? On the mixed-input settings we stress-test---HADES adversarial images paired with harmful text prompts, and spoken AdvBench via text-to-speech (TTS) or silence---text DiM at $T$ raises attack success rate (ASR) while the same mean DiM at $E$/$P$/$F$ does not; attacks track harmful text rather than image or audio content. Margin-rank and leverage probes on a Vision leaf show that this recipe is extremal at $T$ and near chance at $P$/$E$, which pressures a weak-extractor reading of those flat cells for the DiM family we study. Catalog breadth and mapper-free base$\to$derivative transfer when residual widths match provide supporting coverage under the same gates; generative U-Nets are a separate band under generation judges. The primary claim is this recipe-scoped $T$ vs.\ non-text intervenability asymmetry---intervention accessibility under mean / rank-1 DiM, not a claim that refusal is absent or fully represented outside $T$ (text vs.\ perceptual contrasts and pooling differ by site). On VLGuard Unsafe prompts ($n{=}200$; Llama-Guard), the same $T$ vs.\ $P$/$E$ directionality holds at modest absolute ASR ($0.030{\to}0.150$ at $T$). An intervention-oriented Class$\times$site ledger records where this protocol still hooks as supporting coverage, not as a universal multimodal bypass.

items.summary: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. They authenticate to these services with the same bearer secrets humans use, personal access tokens, API keys and package-registry tokens, stored where the model, its subprocesses and any co-resident malware can read them. Incidents in 2025 and 2026, including prompt-injection attacks on coding agents and self-propagating supply-chain worms, show that this arrangement fails in predictable ways. Passkeys solved the analogous problem for humans, but they require a human gesture on every use and cannot be operated by an autonomous process. We present the Agent Authenticator, a design that gives agents passkey-grade authentication properties: per-service hardware-bound keys, no shared secrets, origin binding enforced by the runtime rather than the model, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, and cross-device human approval for high-risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on developer laptops and in cloud enclaves, and it deploys as a profile over existing mechanisms, MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange including the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, git and SSH, rather than as a new identity system. The authenticator also produces a signed, hash-chained record of each action it authorizes. We analyze the design against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, map it onto five documented incidents, and discuss its limits.
items.title: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication for AI Agents

items.summary: An incorrect authorization vulnerability was identified in GitHub Enterprise Server that allowed an authenticated user whose numeric user ID matched an enterprise's numeric ID to manage that enterprise's GitHub Apps and generate private keys without enterprise membership. GitHub App ownership checks compared numeric IDs without checking the owner's account type. Exploitation required control of a session for the colliding user account and an enterprise-owned GitHub App. A generated private key could be used to authenticate as the App and access repositories where it was installed, within its granted permissions. On standard fresh installations, the documented collision involved the non-loginable built-in ghost account; the reported GHES reproduction used site administrator impersonation. This vulnerability affected supported GitHub Enterprise Server releases prior to 3.23 and was fixed in versions 3.19.16, 3.20.12, 3.21.10, and 3.22.5. This vulnerability was reported via the GitHub Bug Bounty program.

items.summary: A path traversal vulnerability (CWE-22) was found in ansible-core's ansible-galaxy role installation. An explicit role "name" taken from a role's meta/requirements.yml is used to construct the on-disk installation path without validating that the resulting destination stays within the selected roles directory. A name containing "../" escapes that directory, and an absolute name replaces it entirely. Because ansible-galaxy processes transitive dependencies from an installed role's meta/requirements.yml, a malicious role publisher can cause attacker-supplied files to be written outside the operator's chosen roles directory when the operator installs the role, and, when --force is used, can cause an existing role directory outside that path to be removed and replaced. The impact is bounded by the invoking user's filesystem permissions and requires the operator to install the attacker-influenced content.

An attacker required an authenticated account, a readable repository and pull request to use as the request context, and target review-thread identifiers. The thread-preview endpoint resolved supplied identifiers without restricting them to the authorized pull request, exposing private file paths and, when positioning and diff data were available, source-code excerpts, commit identifiers, and line metadata without victim interaction. This vulnerability affected supported GitHub Enterprise Server releases in the 3.21, 3.22 series and was fixed in versions 3.21.10, 3.22.5. This vulnerability was reported via the GitHub Bug Bounty program.

items.summary:
Summary

  In multitenant Filament panels, an authenticated user could retrieve media metadata belonging to other tenants
  by typing in the Curator media-picker search box. The search query omitted the tenant ownership scope that the
  normal file listing applies.

  Details

  CuratorPanel::updatedSearch() built its Eloquent query independently of getFiles() and did not apply the
  filament()->hasTenancy() && $isTenantAware tenant-ownership where clause. As a result, the search matched media
  across all tenants. A secondary flaw compounded it: the orWhere('title'…) chain was not wrapped in a nested
  group, so the OR conditions also broke out of the isLimitedToDirectory constraint.

  The issue was introduced in v3.2.4, when multitenancy support was added to the media picker.

  Impact

  - Who: any authenticated user with access to a panel that uses the Curator picker.
  - What: disclosure of other tenants' media metadata (name, title, alt, caption, description, path, etc.)
  returned by the search.
  - Conditions: only affects deployments using Filament multitenancy with Curator's tenant awareness enabled.
  Single-tenant installs are not affected.

  Patches

  Fixed in 3.7.8, 4.1.1, and 5.1.1 by applying the tenant scope to the search query and grouping the search terms
  so they cannot escape the directory/tenant constraints. Upgrade to a patched version.

  Workarounds

  None other than upgrading. Disabling tenant awareness does not help (it removes the boundary entirely).

  Credit

  Reported via coordinated disclosure by [Afsana Alijabarova](https://github.com/afa114).

items.summary:
### Details
When the server acts as the fee_payer, `pympp` 0.8.0 validates calldata using `eth_abi` decoding, which is lenient about trailing bytes. The `FeePayerPolicy` caps `gas_limit` (≤ 2 M) and `max_fee_per_gas` (≤ 100 Gwei) but does **not** check calldata length.

Tempo uses legacy calldata gas pricing: **16 gas per non-zero byte**. Appending `N` bytes of `0x01` padding inflates actual gas used by `N × 16` while keeping `gas_limit` and `max_fee_per_gas` within policy caps. The server cosigns and broadcasts the padded transaction, draining its fee-payer wallet.

**Vulnerable code path:** `FeePayerPolicy` in `fee_payer_policy.py` (pympp 0.8.0) enforces `maxGas = 2_000_000` and `maxFeePerGas = 100 Gwei` but has no `calldata.length` bound. The policy check passes because the inflated gas comes from intrinsic calldata cost, not the declared `gas_limit`.

**Note:** In our experiment, we enforce an 16 KB `max_header_length`, which caps the maximum effective padding at roughly 5,500 bytes. The default padding in this PoC (5,500 bytes) is within that limit.

### PoC
The PoC is provided below. It is configured to reproduce the attack on Tempo Moderate testnet within a Docker environment. Download the PoC and run:
```bash
unzip pympp_python_PoC.zip
cd pympp_python
docker build -t pympp-padding .
docker run --rm pympp-padding
``` 
There are more details in `pympp_python/README.md`

### Impact
In our experiment, a malicious client can force the server to pay ~**5x** the normal transaction fee. This dramatically increases operational costs and completely destroys the profit margin on low-cost items.

Please provide a way to share the PoC in .zip format to you. Thank you!

items.summary:
With Cache Components enabled, an outer `'use cache'` function can be keyed incorrectly even when its inner `'use cache'` call generates a fresh entry. If the inner function reads a root param (via `next/root-params`) and returns a value that still contains pending promises — for example an object with data that is ready immediately alongside slower data — React Flight delivers the ready portion to the outer function before the inner entry has finished publishing its root param dependencies. The outer function can then finish, and its cache entry is persisted under a key that omits that root param. The entry is written once and reused for all root param values, so a response for one root param value can serve content produced for a different value. Entries written this way can also ignore tag invalidation and cache lifetimes of the nested caches they consumed.

What values are leaked cannot be attacker controlled. Which value's content is served depends only on which invocation wrote the entry first.

This is a variant of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h694-7cp9-m8p3 that the fix for that advisory does not cover: it does not require the inner call to be served from an existing entry, and it does not depend on a slow cache handler.
items.title: Next.js: Cache leak across root param values in nested 'use cache' functions via delayed inner stream metadata

items.summary:
## Summary

`qbee-agent` contains a Zip Slip vulnerability in `app/utils/tar.go`. The tar extractor checks whether an entry remains inside the destination directory with:

```go
strings.HasPrefix(targetPath, destdirClean)
```

This does not enforce a path separator boundary. If the destination directory is `/tmp/.../context`, a tar entry such as `../context-outside/payload.txt` cleans to `/tmp/.../context-outside/payload.txt` and still passes the prefix check. qbee-agent then creates the outside directory and writes the payload outside the intended extraction root.

The issue is reachable through the Docker Compose build context path when `UseContext` is enabled.

## Details

Code references below were verified against `qbee-io/qbee-agent` commit:

- `1d8bdbb7422adb4ca563d3114cbe2817d6ba3581`

Affected repository:

- `qbee-io/qbee-agent`

Affected files:

- `app/utils/tar.go`
- Docker Compose context path in `app/configuration/bundle_docker_compose.go`

The vulnerable extraction code:

- `app/utils/tar.go:89-93`

```go
targetPath := filepath.Clean(filepath.Join(destPath, header.Name))
destdirClean := filepath.Clean(destPath)

if !strings.HasPrefix(targetPath, destdirClean) {
    return fmt.Errorf("tar entry %s is outside of destination directory %s", targetPath, destdirClean)
}
```

The file is then created at the accepted `targetPath`:

- `app/utils/tar.go:96-109`

```go
case tar.TypeDir:
    if err := os.MkdirAll(targetPath, 0755); err != nil {
        return err
    }
case tar.TypeReg:
    targetFile, err := os.Create(targetPath)
```

Docker Compose build contexts reach this extractor:

- `app/configuration/bundle_docker_compose.go:238-270`

The context archive is downloaded and then unpacked into the compose project context directory with `utils.UnpackTar`.

Archive source and role evidence:

- `app/configuration/compose.go:14` defines the Docker Compose build context as the remote configuration field `Context string`.
- `app/configuration/compose.go:26` enables this path with `UseContext`.
- `app/configuration/file_manager.go:240-246` and `app/configuration/file_manager.go:281-287` show that context sources are resolved either from `file://` local files or from the Qbee file-manager API.
- Qbee's Docker Compose documentation lists "Build Context" as a Docker Compose configuration option: https://docs.qbee.io/configuration-docker-compose.html
- Qbee's RBAC documentation separates `configuration:manage` from `files:manage`, and maps "Configure -> Modify configuration" to `configuration:manage` while "Files manager -> Write access" maps to `files:manage`: https://docs.qbee.io/account-users-and-roles.html
- Qbee's CI/CD documentation describes using a dedicated Qbee user with a role restricted to configuration changes to push and commit deployment configuration: https://docs.qbee.io/tutorial-iot-container-deployment-with-ci-cd-devops.html

Trust-boundary requirement:

- The vulnerable primitive is clear: qbee-agent writes a regular file outside the intended context extraction directory.
- The security boundary is present when the archive supplier is less privileged than the local qbee-agent process and is not supposed to write arbitrary sibling files in qbee-agent's Docker Compose cache/project area.
- The public code and documentation support this boundary for tenants that delegate configuration and/or file-manager access to limited users or CI automation.
- If a deployment allows only full device/fleet administrators to provide Docker Compose context archives, the finding should be treated as hardening for that deployment.

## PoC

Two failing regression tests add.

The utility-level test proves the extractor bug directly:

- `app/utils/tar_test.go:132`
- `Test_TarZipSlipSiblingPrefixBypass`

Command:

```sh
wsl -e sh -lc 'cd /mnt/c/Users/kwak0/Documents/Qbee/targets/qbee-agent; /mnt/c/Users/kwak0/Documents/Qbee/.tools/go1.26.4-linux/go/bin/go test ./app/utils -run Test_TarZipSlipSiblingPrefixBypass -count=1 -v'
```

items.summary:
### Impact

`write_attachments()` called `_safe_attachment_filename()` and `write_sample()` inside its loop
with no guard, so a single crafted attachment raised out of the whole save. Every attachment
**after** the malicious one was silently never written, with no error surfaced to a caller that
catches only `MailParserError`.

That is an evasion primitive as much as an availability bug: a sender puts one poisoned part
first and the real payload second, and the payload never reaches the extraction directory that
a downstream scanner or sandbox reads — while it still reaches the recipient's mail client
intact. The tool's output diverges from the bytes actually in the message, which is the same
failure mode as the filename-sanitizing bypass in
[GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496](https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496).

Three shapes were reachable, all from attacker-controlled MIME metadata:

- **NUL smuggled through RFC 2231** — `filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin` decodes to a NUL in the
  filename during parsing and raised `ValueError` out of the name check;
- **overlong basename** — a filename longer than `NAME_MAX` (e.g. 300 characters) raised
  `OSError: File name too long` from `open()`, *after* creating a zero-byte stub on disk;
- **undecodable payload** — a body that is not valid base64 raised `binascii.Error` (a
  `ValueError` subclass) from the decode performed inside the `open()` block.

```python
import tempfile, mailparser

raw = ("Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=b\r\n\r\n"
       "--b\r\nContent-Type: application/octet-stream\r\n"
       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin\r\n\r\nxx\r\n"
       "--b\r\nContent-Type: application/octet-stream\r\n"
       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=good.bin\r\n\r\nyy\r\n"
       "--b--\r\n")

mp = mailparser.parse_from_string(raw)     # parse itself is fine; safe_filename is None
mp.write_attachments(tempfile.mkdtemp())
# 4.6.0 - 4.6.2 -> ValueError, and good.bin is never written
# 4.6.3         -> logs "Skipped attachment with invalid filename: 'evil\x00.bin'";
#                  good.bin is written
```

`parse()` itself was never affected — it catches the `ValueError` — so only the write path was
unguarded. The reject-paths that made this reachable were introduced with the filename
sanitizing in 4.6.0 (PR #165).

### Patches

Fixed in **4.6.3**. `write_attachments()` now logs and skips a single unusable attachment
instead of aborting the batch:

- an invalid filename is caught and skipped;
- overlong basenames are truncated to 240 UTF-8 bytes, preserving the extension, rather than
  reaching `open()`;
- the base64 decode moved *before* `open()`, so a failure leaves no zero-byte stub, and it now
  repairs padding and alphabet errors the way mail clients do (matching `MIME::Base64` on 2008
  cases) — rejecting them let a sender append one character to make an attachment vanish from
  the extraction directory while it still reached the recipient;
- `MailParserPathError` is deliberately **not** caught by the per-attachment handler: a
  containment failure is not a per-attachment problem, and path-containment checks now raise
  `MailParserPathError` instead of `ValueError` so the broader catch cannot swallow them.

Deduplication was hardened in the same change: it reserves room for its own suffix marker
(`write_sample()` sanitizes again, and the clamp there used to cut the marker back off,
collapsing distinct attachments onto one file), resumes from the last used suffix per stem
instead of rescanning from 1 (quadratic before — 16000 same-named attachments took 14 s, now
milliseconds), and folds case, because APFS, exFAT and SMB collapse `Invoice.pdf` and
`invoice.pdf`.

### Workarounds

Upgrade to 4.6.3. If you cannot upgrade, do not call `write_attachments()` on untrusted mail;
iterate `parser.attachments` yourself and write each attachment inside its own
`try`/`except Exception`, skipping the ones whose `sa

items.summary:
**Ecosystem / package:** Go — `github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark` (the `kubeshark`
CLI, `kubeshark mcp` subcommand)
**Affected component:** `cmd/mcpRunner.go`, MCP tool `download_file`
**Affected versions:** `>= v53.1.0`, `< v53.4.0` (the flaw shipped with the
tool's first release; v53.3.0 was the last affected release)
**Patched version:** `v53.4.0`
**Credit:** novice-22 (Urim), via private coordinated disclosure.

## Summary
The `download_file` MCP tool fetches a caller-supplied `path` from the Kubeshark
Hub API and writes the response body to a caller-supplied `dest` on the local
filesystem with no validation of `dest`. An attacker who can influence the MCP
tool arguments — e.g. via indirect prompt injection against an AI agent driving
`kubeshark mcp` — can write attacker-controlled bytes to an arbitrary path
writable by the user running the MCP server (e.g. `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`,
`~/.kube/config`, `~/.bashrc`), and can request arbitrary Hub API endpoints.
`download_file` is registered unconditionally (available in the default,
non-`--allow-destructive` posture).

## Introduced in
Commit `eb7dc42b` — "Add get_file_url and download_file MCP tools (#1853)",
2026-03-04 — first released in **v53.1.0** (`v53.1.0~1`). An earlier attempt
(`dbfd17d9`) was reverted (`a46f05c4`) before any release, so no tag before
v53.1.0 is affected.

## Details
In `callDownloadFile` (`cmd/mcpRunner.go`), both `path` and `dest` come straight
from the tool arguments:
- `dest` was passed directly to `os.Create(dest)` with no confinement — no
  `filepath.Clean`, no base-directory containment, no rejection of absolute

- `path` was concatenated onto the Hub API base URL with no allowlist, so any

The tool originally issued the fetch with no authentication. The authentication

forwards the operator's Hub credentials (ServiceAccount token / License-Key) and
rejects auth-required responses instead of writing a login page to disk. **But**
the Hub ships auth-disabled by default (community/dev), so on a default
`kubeshark tap` the Hub API answers without authentication and captured traffic
(credentials/tokens/PII) can still be read and exfiltrated end-to-end. Enforcing
Hub auth by default is tracked separately (gated-auth workstream) and is **not**
part of this advisory's fix.

Following the tool's documented workflow on a default community install:

- **Integrity (local):** arbitrary file write on the machine running

- **Confidentiality:** read of Hub API endpoints, incl. captured network traffic

- Reliable RCE is not demonstrated (script endpoints are JSON-wrapped).

items.summary:
A path traversal vulnerability was identified in mail-parser when extracting email attachments using the write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

A specially crafted email containing malicious attachment filenames (for example, using directory traversal sequences such as "../" or absolute filesystem paths) could cause files to be written outside the intended output directory. Depending on how the library was used and the permissions of the executing process, this could result in arbitrary file overwrite.

The vulnerability affects mail-parser versions 3.8.0 through 4.5.0.

The issue has been addressed by introducing comprehensive filename sanitization and path validation before any file is written to disk. The fix includes:

- Sanitization of attachment filenames before writing.
- Validation that all output paths remain within the intended destination directory.
- Rejection of symbolic link targets.
- Normalization of Windows and POSIX path separators.
- Validation and rejection of invalid or unsafe filenames.
- Protection applied consistently in both write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

Users are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the patched release.

## Credits

The vulnerability was responsibly reported by **Niranjan Ganesan** (Security Insights, https://securityinsights.io/, GitHub: @iam-niranjan).

The vulnerability was analyzed, remediated, and the security fix was implemented by **Fedele Mantuano**, maintainer of mail-parser (LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/fmantuano/).

mail-parser would like to thank Niranjan Ganesan for following a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process and for collaborating throughout the remediation and verification of the fix.

items.summary: Nuxt is an open-source web development framework for Vue.js. Nuxt from 3.0.0 until 4.6.4, @nuxt/nitro-server from 3.20.0 until 4.6.4, and @nuxt/vite-server from 4.6.0 until 4.6.4, routeRules matching leaves an encoded slash (%2F) in the request path while a catch-all page such as app/pages/[...slug].vue or a custom multi-segment page route decodes it into a route parameter. The getRouteRules result is therefore incomplete, and an unauthenticated request can render the page without the redirect, headers, proxy, SSR, noScripts, appMiddleware, or appLayout rules configured for the decoded path. Protected content is resolved only when the page interprets the decoded parameter accordingly: a custom multi-segment parameter can contain the decoded path, while a repeatable catch-all must join the slash-containing array element; route.path remains encoded and does not resolve that resource. Static pages, single-segment parameters, server/api handlers, and server/routes handlers are not affected because they do not have the same encoded-path mismatch. This issue is fixed in version 4.6.4.
